BRODEUR (Minister of Mar rine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 152) to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. He said: The object is to give a better definition of the word 'vessel' in the Act. A wrecked vessel is there defined to include merely the keel, hull and machinery, but not the equipment, tackle, cargo, stores and ballast. When a vessel is wrecked, they generally remove at once all that is of value in it, and nothing is left except the hull and machinery, which is most of the time not of much value. Consequently when we call for tenders for the removal of a wreck, we have to deal with an article which is almost of no value and becomes a loss to the country; and the object is to declare that when a vessel is wrecked, the cargo should not be removed but form part of the claim which must exist on the vessel for the cost of removal of the wreckage. We ask also to be allowed to amend the law in order to declare that wrecks shall be removed immediately without the necessity of obtaining a formal order in council, but simply on the order of the minister. The reason for the change is this: When a wreck takes place, it sometimes is absolutely necessary to have it removed without delay, but when we have to go before the Governor in Council some time is lost. It may take a good deal of time before we can get an order in council, and in the meantime navigation may be seriously affected. We are asking also for power to regulate the cables which are
put in rivers for ferry-boats. The request to do this has been made to the government by different provinces and especially by the province of Manitoba. In that province the complaint is made that cables are put in some of its navigable rivers and there is no provision in the law to regulate them. The object is to provide that they shall only be laid in such a way as not to interfere with navigation. We wish also to improve the regulations for the opening and closing of draw-bridges and their operation. This gives power to the government to make some regulations in that connection.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 153) respecting the National Transcontinental Railway. He said: This is a very trifling Bill. A bridge has to be constructed over the Red river between the cities of Winnipeg and St. Bonifice by the Transcontinental Commission. These cities are anxious to make some arrangement by which they can construct a bridge for vehicles as well in connection with this bridge. The legislature of Manitoba has given the city of Winnipeg the power to make such an arrangement if it can, and this will allow the Intercolonial Railway Commission to make arrangements, if they think it is advisable, for the construction of a traffic bridge in connection with the railway.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 154) to amend the Act respecting the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. He said: The object is to ex tend the boundaries of the harbour of Montreal. To-day these boundaries extend from Verdun to Longue Point, and it is proposed to continue them from Longue Point to the extreme north eastern end of the island. We are also seeking power to declare that the port of Montreal shall be in the future under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The port of Montreal is now that part of the River St. Lawrence which extends from Portneuf to Montreal. That part of the river was declared some years ago the port of Montreal for pilotage purposes. In 1903, a change was made by which the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal ceased to be the pilot-

age authority, and that authority was then vested in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. No change, however, was made in the law itself, and as we are amending the law this year for the purposes that I have just mentioned, I thought it would be just as well to declare that the port of Montreal should, in that respect, cease to be under the control of the Harbour Commissioners. As a matter of fact, that has already been done. However, the right to make the rules of the road on that part of the river has hitherto been exercised by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. In all other ports of this country, the rules of the road are made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and it was thought advisable, as the harbour commissioners had ceased to be the pilotage authority, that the rules of the road should be made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, as is the case in all the other navigable waters. These are the only changes proposed, except a small change declaring beyond doubt that the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal have the right to operate railways within the limits of the harbour.
, Mr. MONK. Are we to understand that the commission itself is to be abolished and the department to take over the entire management of the port?

Oh no, the Bill simply provides that the commissioners will cease to exercise any authority with regard to the rules of the road and pilotage in the port of Montreal; as; to the management of the harbour itself the authority of the existing Harbour Commission will continue.
Is it intended by this resolution to give effect to the report of the Transportation Commission that the port of Montreal be made a national and a free port?

I do not understand that the Transportation Commission ever asked that it be made a free port. I know it was suggested it should be made a national port, but it is not the intention by this Bill to make any change in that respect.
Did the commission not recommend that the port be made a free pori?
I do not remember that.

Before the Bill is read the first time I wish to make a suggestion for the consideration of the minister. I would ask him to consider the advisability of extending the jurisdiction of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal to the south side of the St. Lawrence. Their jurisdiction now extends, I believe, only to the centre of the river. The business of Mr. BRODEUR .
the harbour of Montreal has increased so that the harbour is now somewhat congested and the change I suggest would undoubtedly be an advantage. They might be given jurisdiction over the south shore of that part of the river commencing at the Victoria bridge and including St. Lambert, Longueuil and Boucherville. With comparatively little dredging a channel could be provided affording navigation there, and wharfs and probably elevators could be built which would relieve the congestion now existing in the harbour of Montreal. I do not see why we have not navigation upon that side of the St. Lawrence. St. Lambert is a town which is increasing rapidly and so is Longueuil. The minister knows that there are several railways now in those towns. The Delaware and Hudson Railway is building a very important road from Montreal to Quebec. Then we have the Grand Trunk Railway and several American railways besides the Intercolonial Railway, all coming to St. Lambert and an electric railway will soon connect the town with Montreal. That part of the St. Lawrence is fast increasing in importance and I think it would be to the general advantage if jurisdiction over it were vested in the Montreal Harbour Commission. I hope the minister will take this matter into consideration and consult the Harbour Commissioners, who have promised to consider it. Of course I do not make this proposition solely for the advantage of that part of the country; the suggested change would also be of advantage to the port and city of Montreal because it would be very easy to build elevators there which cannot be built on the Montreal side.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me we are drifting into a general discussion.
This is the first reading of the Bill.
It is perfectly in order.

The minister has explained his Bill and before he proceeds with it I wish to make a suggestion and to 'explain to him as fully as possible the advantages to be derived from my suggestion. The minister knows that the valleys of the St. Lawrence and the Richelieu are probably the most fertile and prosperous
arts of the province of Quebec and now
e has an opportunity to come to our relief. We have been deprived of all these communications with the city of Montreal and it is thought that if jurisdiction over the south shore was vested in the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal there would very soon be a great change in that part of the country. I need not go further at present as the Bill will come up for discussion in the committee. I hope the minister will be able to favourably consider

my suggestion before the Bill again comes before us.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

SHARPE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 155) to amend the Bank Act. He said: The provisions of this Bill are very simple. It merely provides that the balances that remain in the hands of chartered banks for over six years shall be transferred to the government as trustees and custodians of a fund on behalf of those entitled to them. The Bill is very-simple.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

I will attend to that this afternoon.

I would call the attention of the minister to the return brought down from the Transcontinental Commissioners with reference to the employments and
employees. There is one schedule they do not fill out, they say it will take two or three weeks to get the information. I would like the minister to inform them that the information is required, and that the return is not satisfactory without that.
As to the residences?

speechtext: I desire to call to the notice of the Minister of Railways and Canals a matter under the Railway Act that seems to be ground for complaint in several parts of the country, that is, in respect to the powers of expropriation of lands for right of way by railway companies. There is provision in section 122 of the Railway Act which provides that the price of lands taken for right of way shall be the value of the land at the time that certain plans and specifications were filed in the registry of deeds for the district in which the lands lie. It is said that that provision, and that privilege, is being abused by certain railway companies, who put their plans on record and then allow the matter to stand for an indefinite period.
No debate can take place at this point of our proceedings.

Then I would ask the Minister if he thinks that any remedy could be applied, so that the company would be compelled to proceed with the expropriation, as seems to be the intention of the Act, and not be allowed to wait for an indefinite time.

That matter has been engaging the attention of the department for some little time. In an amendment to the Railway Act I have introduced, I have a clause dealing with that, which I think will remedy the real evil complained of by my hon. friend.

As a new member of the House I have listened very attentively to the various speeches that have been delivered on this motion. What has struck me most forcibly is the wonderful difference of opinion expressed by hbn. members on both sides of the House. I cannot say I am surprised at that, because we know that it is very seldom indeed that many people agree entirely on any financial matter. That fact proves the absolute necessity of having at the head of the finances of this country a man that we have faith in.
I can certainly say that of the hon. Minister of Finance who has had charge of the finances of this country for the last twelve years. Personally I am willing to acknowledge that it would be difficult to find any other gentleman in the whole country more capable than the present Minister of Finance to look after our finances, both as regards the revenue received and the expenditure. Hence we see the necessity of having a supreme head of the finances in whom we have confidence.
After listening to the criticisms of hon. members on the other side of the House, and leaving out of view the superfluity of words and the extra flow of language which characterized them, they practically amount to two charges, namely, that our expenditure has been too high, and that our loans have cost us too much to float, thereby impairing the credit of Canada. Even the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), if you make deduction of the vivid imagery and dramatic eloquence with which his speech abounded, only added a warning to the Finance Minister that the American people will probably adopt a maximum and a minimum tariff. I would like to look at the cost of the loans for the last few years. I am not going into figures very mudh, because you know the old adage that figures cannot lie, as stated by some wise man in the past, and also the equally old adage that you can prove anything by figures. Therefore, I am going to look at it, as far as I can, from the simple, practical, eveTy day business man's standpoint. The cost of loans since 1897, some hon. gentlemen say, has very much exceeded the cost of loans previous to that time. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has told us, and I think quite correctly, that the loan that was floated in 1897 was an exceptional loan, that it was an exceptional period and all of us who have kept track of the loan market for a number of years will fully agree with him that the period from 1896 really until 1902 inclusive was an exceptional period in the history of the world as far as the interest cost on loans was concerned.

The hon. member for North Toronto has stated that the cost of floating the loans of this government has exceeded the cost of floating the loans of the Conservative government previously in all instances except in that one case. I have, since that speech was made, looked carefully into the cost of floating the loans and I think that the cost is exactly the same as it was at that time, but that the system of making the loans has very materially changed. It would be idle for us to deny, if we have followed the loan market for any length of time, that the system of making loans has changed. No Minister of Finance can regulate that. The fact is that you have to adapt yourself to the system in vogue at the time and, of recent years, the system has been that you have to go to the underwriters. The reason for that is very simple. The loaning public have faith in some underwriter who has made a reputation for himself, and he passes on the loan practically speaking before it goes to the general public. I do not know that that is a wise precaution. I believe it is	but,	in	anyevent, it is the	system	that	is	invogue at the present time and it is a system that has to be followed not only by large corporations, such as railway and loan corporations, but by governments. It is the only system that you can take advantage of. The reason why interest has been so much	dearer	than	it	wasin 1897, is because the loan market has run higher. Under	this system	of	underwriting, loans that are put on the market are scrutinized by the underwriters and the public therefore take hold of them. There is more competition in the loan market and in making a loan on behalf of the country or on behalf of any institution you have to bid against the competition. You have to be governed by that competition. That is no reason to say that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has not done just as well with the loans that he has floated for this country as any person else could have done, and I believe he has done better than could have been done by almost any person else. However, he has done all that could be done and our loans have not suffered in comparison with similar loans that have been floated by other countries. We all know that Japan, Russia, Germany and the great countries of Europe have paid more for their loans than we have paid during the same period. What more could you say to the credit of the Finance Minister in floating these loans?
The hon. member for North Toronto says that the Minister of Finance says that in calculating the cost to the people of this country it is not fair to say that the indebtedness per capita is a proper criterion to take. He says that even if we do calculate on a less rate per dollar it costs $11
per head to live. I think that one of the most creditable things that can be said of the Liberal party in governing this country is that the people had means enough to pay the greater amount, had means enough to purchase sufficient goods which they did at a lower rate on the dollar. Even if the cost were $11 per head as against $6.50 per head it reflects all the more credit upon this party that the people were able to purchase that much more goods. The hon. member for North Toronto says that the wise business man, when he makes his calculations for the year, sits down and figures what goods he is going to require; that is his raw material, I suppose, if he be a manufacturer, and his stock in trade, if he be a merchant. He also figures or estimates the amount of business that he is going to do. The hon. member for North Toronto says that we do not do so. It is quite true that any reasonably decent business man does estimate what the cost of his voods is going to be, does estimate what quantity of goods he is going to require during the next year and what his sales are going to be. But, that is only an estimate after all. He does not absolutely know. There are few business men who know the year before the quantity of goods that they aTe going to put out next year. There are some business men and some manufacturers who have to estimate three and four years ahead what goods or what raw material they are going to require. Supposing that the hard times came would not they also have incurred expense that the hon. member for North Toronto might equally as well say should have been avoided? The Minister of Finance can only make estimates, but there are certain forced expenditures which not only this government, but every other government in the world finds it impossible to foresee. The mother country has been forced to tax more than she would like to tax. Every country in Europe is forced to tax until the people are almost broken down to meet military and naval expenditures. In our country, while we have no military or naval expenditures, look at the transportation that we have to provide for.
Look at the various other expenditures that are absolutely forced upon the government, whether they will or not It is unfair criticism to say that many of the public expenditures ought to have been cut off some years ago, because every intelligent business man knows that you cannot cut off a business in the middle of its operations. Every member of this House who knows anything about business, and I think most of us do, knows that in the year 1907 and the first part of 1908 the great industrial and transportation corporations of the country would like to have cut down their expenditure, but they found it impossible to do so. No matter how prescient

they may have been they could not have foreseen the hard times of 1907 and 1908, and although many of them, as early as July and August, 1907, saw the depression coming, yet they had their output provided for and they had contracts for supplies let and they had to carry on their business as they had been doing in the past. How could the Minister of Finance have foreseen these times of stress any more than the great captains of industry in the commercial world. But, the hon. gentleman did as other prudent men and he now has wisely reduced the public expenditure. The government had made preparations for certain expenditures, just as business people had, and if they had stayed their hand and interrupted the progress of the country to that extent, I can imagine how hon. gentlemen opposite would have raised their voices to Heaven in denunciation of such a policy. The hon. member for North Toronto quoted some figures from a little book published by Mr. Woods of Toronto, and as I remember the figures quoted by the hon. gentleman they went to show that during the last four years $802,000,000 had been the extent of the borrowings all over this country. I have no doubt these figures are perfectly correct, and if the hon. member (Mr. Foster) or any other man had wanted to preach a sermon from the Epistle of Fielding to the Canadians he could not have taken a more appropriate text to prove the prosperity of this country. What enabled the people of this country to borrow that great sum in four years if it was not that the wise policy of the government had firmly established the credit of Canada and of Canadian concerns on the money markets of the world?

My hon. friend misapprehended the statement and therefore his argument does not rest on a sound foundation. I did not take it upon myself to say, nor did Mr. Woods, that this country had in eight years borrowed $802,000,000. That would have been a most extraordinary thing.
That is what I understood the hon. gentleman to say.

My hon. friend is mistaken. What Mr. Woods said was that at a certain date, I think the 31st of December, 1908, that was the amount of bonds of three denominations that were now running, but many of them may have been borrowed sixteen or twenty years ago.

Well, Mr. Speaker, we have it Stated by a reliable financial authority that Canada borrowed all told $650,000,000 last year, and therefore my argument is still sound, that the high standing of this country has been so established under the wise policy of the Liberal government that the credit of our railway corporations, our industrial corporations, our mining Mr. NESBITT.
companies, and all other concerns, is so high that they were able to borrow this vast sum, and even to become competitors of the Dominion government in the borrowing market. It is not so many years ago since the only loans that could be floated in Canada at any reasonable interest were the loans made by the Dominion government. But now, any reasonable proposition coming from Canada is so highly regarded not only in England but in Germany and France that it can obtain money just as easily as can the Dominion government, or for that matter the British government itself. And why is that? It is because the policy of the Canadian government has been so wise and so progressive that Canadian concerns are no longer confined to the money markets of England, or of the United States, or of Canada, but can go to France or to Germany and raise money with the greatest facility. France is probably the greatest lending country in the world and to-day the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway is sold in France as readily as in England. This again is a tribute to the policy of the government which has laid so solidly the credit of Canadian business enterprises. One hon. member on the other side told us that a week ago in New York money was loaned at 1} per cent and 15 per cent, but that money was raised on call loans and everybody knows that call loans in New York are sometimes down as low as even 1 per cent. But that is an entirely different proposition from business loans. At the very time when call loans are going at 1 per cent let any man try to float on the same market a time loan for 30 or 40 years, and he will see what he will have to nay for it. One hon. gentleman ormosite cites the instance of a three months' loan which had been floated in New York the other day, but what has that to do with the question? A loan for three months is a very short date loan. Any reasonable ordinary man can say what the money market is going to be for three months; but how many men dare say what the money market is going to be for five years from now, let alone for forty years from now? How many people are going to risk their money in long-time loans when there are more demands for money all the time on things which are absolutely safe, so far as things can be safe in this world, and paying them five or six per cent interest? Do you expect our Minister of Finance to float loans against the demands of other countries or corporations, and float them cheaner than they do? If so, you expect something that no human being can do, and I suppose our Minister of Finance does not claim to be more than human.
The hon. Minister of Finance has been criticised for having floated shoTt-date loans. I submit that that is purely and simply an opinion. I might express the op-

posite opinion. Any gentleman on either side of the House oan express opinions or make assertions, but that does not make them true. During the last few years, while money has been high, I think, with all due deference, that the Finance Minister was wise in not trying to negotiate long-time loans when he did not know the moment the money market would be in a more satisfactory condition. It is all very well to point out that he paid li per cent commission on those loans; but suppose he had paid 2 per cent. That is 2 per cent on only one year, on the face amount of the loan, which means that if he got a loan for 20 years or 30 years, the 2 per cent of cost would be wiped out at i per cent per year in four years, and for the balance of the period there would be a profit to us.
One hon. member, in the effort to show that our credit was impaired, said that the Bank of British North America had, on some day. written off a certain proportion on some bonds of Canada which it held, because they were depreciated in value, but had not written off British consols. Is that a fair criticism? British consols, if they do belong to old England, are on exactly the .same basis as our bonds. If that bank chose to write off our securities, and did not choose to write off British consols, is that any reason why it could not have done so ? That is only the opinion of the manager of one bank; and while I have a great deal of respect for experience and for the opinions of some bank managers, there are others for whose opinions I have not so much respect-and they only have their opinion, after all. So I do* not think that is a fair criticism. If you go back over the last ten or twelve years, and follow Canadian government securities on the British market, you will find that they have not fluctuated as much as British consols; and I have at no time noticed that the securities of any country, of the same class, have been in better demand than the securities of the Dominion of Canada during that time. That is what speaks. _ It is not what we can borrow money for; it is what we can borrow money for in comparison with other people on an equal basis.
This brings me to a suggestion. I believe, with one of the hon. members on the other side of the House, and with my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), in sinking fund loans. I have always believed in them. It is quite true that we are getting value for our money in the promotion of the transportation of this country, and in various public works we are building, and that the future should pay for_ these, at any rate to a large extent. It is also true that the future commences to-morrow. Therefore we should, in my judgment, commence to pay for them, or prepare to pay for them, at least partially, to-morrow. When a loan is floated, we should at once 152

begin to prepare for payment. I do not believe we should borrow money-and if you take the Finance Minister's report, you will find that we do not for building ordinary public works sucn as public buildings. I believe we should pay for these as we go along; but for great public works such as we are forced to build to maintain the progress of the oountry, there is no Teason why posterity should not help to pay; and I believe that every man who has studied finance to any extent at all, will agree with that.
Some hon. members on the other side of the House say that we should not have cut down our expenditures on ordinary public works. There is a good deal in that argument, because during the last two years we could have built very much more cheaply than we did in the previous five or six years. But the hon. Finance Minister did not think it wise, nor did any of his supporters, that that should have been done, and we are perfectly willing to abide by his opinion.
One hon. member the other night said that the Bank of Montreal has refused loans to private corporations because this government had borrowed during 1907 or 1908, $20,000,000. The hon. Finance Minister challenged him at the time to say if he had ever been told that by an authority in the Bank of Montreal. The hon. gentleman did not answer that question. That was a very unfair criticism. I do not think, nor do I believe that he or any other man in this House thinks, that it was because of the borrowings of the Dominion government from the Bank of Montreal that loans were refused to private customers. Every member of this House knows that the reason why the banks refused to advance more money to private customers was that they thought that the manufacturers and merchants of this country were promoting their businesses too rapidly, and that the banks should check them a little-probably a very wise precaution under the circumstances. Everybody knows that it was the actual money itself which was scarce. Everybody knows that the banks were not afraid to make loans but were afraid that the money might be called for. The money however, was not actually taken out of the hands of the Bank of Montreal by the Dominion government. The banks did not think that the money would be taken out and put into the 'minister's pocket or hidden in some cellar. They were not afraid of that, so that I do not believe that the criticism was a fair one.
The hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) sounded the warning, with reference to the tariff, that the United States will apply their maximum unless we give them the same preference as we give the French. Well, so far as I have seen in I the papers, the question of a maximum

and minimum tariff has not as yet been brought up in the American Senate, and is not at all settled. Was there any particular necessity for the warning? If you take the French treaty and see the articles on which France is given a preference over and above every other country except the mother country, and by the way the hon. gentleman said that they were even given a preference over the British, but if you will go through the schedule carefully, as I have done, you will only find two items of which that can be said, and those are two that we never have imported from Great Britain. You will see that should the United States apply their maximum tariff to us unless we give them the French preference tariff, there are very few items in the preference we give the French which we import from the United States. It is true that the minimum tariff, applied to a great many articles under the French treaty, would affect us to a large extent, if brought in from the United States, but I do not see that there will be any difficulty in arranging with the United States when the time comes for doing so.
Now, with reference to the Finance Minister himself, when we come to consider the pressure brought on him, both by members on the opposite side as on this, to change the tariff in the interest of some particular locality or corporation or individuals, we must give him great credit for the stability he has put into our tariff. And after all we must admit that stability in our tariff is the main thing in keeping faith with the rest of the world. We cannot go on changing our tariff daily, we cannot keep tinkering at it every year, without doing harm to some particular branch of merchandise, but to merchandise in general.
Again, when we come to consider the pressure brought upon the Finance Minister, not alone by members on this side but by members opposite, to incur large public expenditures-and just as much or practically as much does the pressure come from the other side as from this for extraordinary expenditures in various localities-do you not think that it requires a man of steel, let alone of iron, to withstand that pressure? And then when the Finance Minister does yield to pressure, and when expenditures are incurred, we find these hon. gentlemen opposite, who are urging him to spend the money, crying out to high heaven that he is ruining the country.
I believe that our Finance Minister deserves a great deal of credit for firmness and decision and foresight in administering our finances, and that brings me to the fact that my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) told us that next year we would add $70,000,000 to our national

Mr. Speaker, in this, the 13th week of the session, it is not my purpose to detain the House at any very great length. The Finance Minister m this, the 13th year of his rule and of the regime of the Liberal party, finds that the national debt of Canada has been increasing by leaps and bounds. It seems to me that this unlucky number has been following the hon. gentleman all the way through. Taxation also in this 13th year of Liberal rule is increasing. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) looks at me through his spec-
There is perhaps a context.

The hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) ridiculed the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr Foster) for having a deficit in the latter years of the reign of the Conservative party. By the way, I may remark here that I am going to make a slight difference in my address from nearly every member on the other side of the House, who has made the hon. member for North Toronto the chief figure or text of his speech. I think the hon. member for North Toronto is perfectly able to take care of himself, and I do not propose, during my remarks, to use him simply as a text. I may say however, that I think the hon. member for North Essex might have been a little more fair with the hon. member for North Toronto. He claimed that in the last three years of the Conservative regime there was a deficit of $5,700,000. I grant that was the case; but it only goes to show the wisdom of the Finance Minister of that day A series of bad times, or a depression I

might call it, was setting in about the year 1891. It was evident that the outlook was not very rosy for some years to come, and the Minister of Finance of that day, acting as a wise statesman, says:	We will remove some of the taxes, and leave the money in the pockets of the people; and by a stroke of his pen he struck off the duties on raw sugar, and relieved the people of Canada, in the five years from 1891 to 1896, of a taxation equal to about $19,000,000. Had the Minister of Finance chosen at that time to continue that taxation, to continue the duties on raw sugar, instead of having a deficit of $5,700,000 in those three years, he would have had a very respectable surplus indeed.
Now I am going to repeat some figures that have been given by previous speakers and that are matters of record. I think it is well that these figures should be repeated time and again, that they should be fairly grounded into the minds of the people, in order that they may realize what the financial position of the country is. Away back in 1893 when the famous platform of the Liberal party was formed, they made the declaration that they viewed with alarm the continual increase of the national debt. In 1896 the debt of the country, when the Conservatives left power, was $258,500,000; in 1909, according to the estimate given us by the Finance Minister, our net debt has increased to $323,960,000, an increase during the regime of the Liberal party of $65,460,000. I wonder if they view that with alarm. Are they going to repeat the old expression, 'We view with alarm the continuous increase of the national debt of the country.' ? I have not heard from one of them that expression during these four days of debate.
We have something to show for it.

The Minister of Customs says that they have something to show for it. Did not the Conservative party have something to show for their national debt? The Conservative party had completed a transcontinental railway, they had purchased a country, they had put through a railway to the Pacific Ocean, and it was in operation. They were not only taking people into that country, but they were bringing out their products. They had something to show for their expenditure, certainly. Now, let me point to this debt in another way, because, as I said, I think it ought to be ground into the minds of the people, and we cannot do it better than by way of illustration. The net debt in 1908 was $40.49 per head of the population of this country. In one year it has risen to $45.72, an increase of nearly $5 per head of the population. Then, as I hear, and as we will no doubt hear from some
hon. members on the other side of the House:	'Wait till you see us next year.'
Now, one word about expenditure. In 1896, the last year of the rule of the Conservative party, the expenditure on capital and consolidated revenue accounts was $44,000,000. In 1898 it reached, within a few thousand dollars of the enormous sum of $113,000,000, an increase of $69,000,000. I doubt very much even if hon. gentlemen sitting on your right, Mr. Speaker, have realized that this ought to be viewed with alarm. Speaking of undue taxation, which they also viewed with alarm in 1893, the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir -Wilfrid Laurier) stated that 'we are a party of low taxation.' The taxation for customs and excise in 1896 was $27,758,285, or $5.46 per head of the population. In 1908, for customs and excise, we paid $73,023,046, or $11.70 per head of the population. I ask hon. gentlemen if this is not a very considerable increase. Is it not enough to cause them to pause and view with alarm the condition to which they are bringing the affairs of this country. But I think a more impressive way still to grind that into the minds of the people of this country, in order that they may realize whither we are drifting, is this: In 1896 the total taxation per family was $27.68, but in 1908 it had increased to $58.88. Let us look at the daily tax. In 1908 the taxation per week was $1,404,289, while it had only been $503,877 in 1896. The taxation per day, Sunday included, on account of customs and excise in 1908 amounted to $200,612, whereas, in 1896, it only amounted to $76,281. I think that the people of this country might well view that with alarm also. But, the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) had another way of telling this story in bygone years. Those of us who were in parliament prior to 1896 did not hear the Minister of Customs speaking of the average rate of taxation on goods coming into the country, dutiable and free, and making a comparison from year to year. He then preferred to make his comparison on the basis of so much per head of the population of the country. In 1896 the customs taxation alone amounted to $3.94 per head, in 1906 it had risen to $7.70, and in 1908 it had risen to $9.26. The Minister of Customs has abandoned that plan of showing the taxation of the country. He found it was telling hard against this government; so, he has fallen back upon another plan, that of taking the average rate of taxation on goods dutiable and free. sorry for the country. I believe that the hon. gentleman is libelling his country.
That is all changed now.

Yes, that is all changed and it was changed before the hon. gentleman came to this countay. That was changed before the Conservative party went out of power. Why, the Conservative party bought that country and paid for it-no they charged it to capital account which I think was a very good thing. It is not paid for yet. It simply cost us the interest on the money. I believe that was a very good plan. Canada was not as rich in those days as it is now, but the government of that day not only bought the country but built the railway to take the hon. gentleman out theTe and bring his products into the markets for which he ought to be reasonably thankful. If it had not been that the Conservative party was in power before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clark) came to this country I doubt very much if he would have his 1,000 acres of farm land that he boasts so much of. He ought to be proud that the Conservative party once ruled in this oountry. Now, I want to show the hon. gentleman that he is all wrong, and to do that I will tell him how his friend gets along. His friend comes home weary from work and his wife is preparing the rabbit for supper, and he sits down in a comer of the kitchen to have a smoke and he sees that the plug of tobacco instead of the large plug it was in the Conservative days is very much smaller and is in fact what the people of Nova Scotia cadi the ' Fielding fig.' He finds around him that everything has been increased in duty but at last he says: 'Heaven be thankful that there is no duty on the light.' His good wife points out that he is mistaken and she says to him: 'Why, this government that you sent the member for Red Deer to support actually increased from 15 per cent to 25 per cent the duty on the putty that keeps the glass of the window in its place.' They rise in the morning and their frugal meal is prepared and the good man says:	'There is no duty on oatmeal,'
but his wife tells him that the government

he is supporting, two or three years ago increased the duty on the Scotchman's oatmeal from 20 per cent up to 60 cents per 100 pounds. This tariff is a tariff for revenue only; it may be but it is not a tariff for the settler. After breakfast the friend of the member for Red Deer goes out to the stable to hitch up his horse, and looking at the cement,on the stable floor he finds that this government has increased the duty on cement five cents per barrel, for the benefit of the farmers I suppose. He sees that the duty on his cutter is increased from 25 to 35 per cent, but he can console himself with the thought that the Minister of Finance has advised him to buy his cutters in England when he will get the benefit of the preferential tariff. He remembers that in the west he is a long way from England, that the transportation charges would be pretty high on cutters, and that as the lesser of two evils he had better pay the full duty on them.
They buy their linen in England.

Oh yes, that is where they buy their linen but the linen manufacturer in the old country makes U3 pay for it with an increased price on his linen. Did we not hear the Minister of Finance tell us how they played a trick with the sugar duties, and before I get through I will explain to the Minister of Customs that there is a corresponding actual increase in the cost of linen sent to this country, over what there would be were it not for the preferential tariff. Now, furs are necessary in the west for the farmer and his wife, and they find that for their fur coats and fur mitts and the fur sleigh robe to keep them warm they have to pay an increased duty of five per cent over what they paid in the Conservative days. Then the farmer says: 'what does all this mean?' and the wife tells him just as the member for Red Deer told us:	'It is a tariff for

When did I say so?
Always.
Before I have finished my speech, I will tell the Minister of Customs what I would like, but in the meantime I prefer to make my own speech.
I beg your pardon.

Why, great heavens, we cannot make the tariff higher on some things than you have got it now. If you import linen from Germany you pay 40 per cent, and if you import cotton from Germany you pay 40 per cent, and I can tell my hon. friend the Minister of Customs
that many of the people in this country have but a small conception of what this tariff for revenue only really is.
Woollens from Germany are 45 per cent.

They possibly are, but we do not bring many of them from Germany; your tariff is too high, we cannot get over it. My hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) told us that the farmers were not worrying. Well, I do not know why they should, because when the Conservative party was in power they gave them a tariff that suited them and that tariff practically remains intact to-day. It has not been greatly disturbed by the peculiar dealings of the present government, and with the exception of two articles, mutton and corn, the tariff just remains about where the Conservative party left it. Now, let me proceed with my illustration. The good farmer says to his wife: 'But has the government done nothing for the farmers?' and she answers, 'Oh yes. cultivators, seed drills, horse rakes, and wagons, have the same duty now as when the Conservatives were in power, but the Liberals have reduced he duty on sickles, and scythes, and snaths, and reaping hooks, and hand rakes, and they have put mushroom spawn and sausage skins and mustard seed on the free list just to please the hon. member for Red Deer who no doubt is duly thankful. 'When the hon. gentleman goes back to Red Deer he had better tell his friends that he will have to change his way of voting if he wants to have a low tariff.

Will the hon. member permit me to ask him if he was correctly reported in ' Hansard ' as having said a few years ago in the budget debate that if he had fifty majority on that side of the House, he would soon repeal the British preference, which I claim to be something for the benefit of the farmer?

My memory is too short-I have no recollection of having made the statement. If the hon. gentleman says I did make it, I will certainly agree to it. I will give him my views of the preferential tariff before I am through. I know that I have been challenged by the Minister of Finance to say whether I would repeal the British preference or not, and I might have made that statement.
The Minister of Customs clings to the idea that this is a low rate of taxation. He adheres to his plan of measuring the taxation of the country by the average rate of duty. In getting at this, the hon. minister simply takes the table of averages previous to the Conservatives going out of power and the table of averages after the Liberals came into power, but he neglects to arrange these tables on the same basis.

We know that the system of taxation in this country has been very materially changed, in many ways. Last year $2,000,000 was added on tobacco; but that has been collected as excise duty, so that if it does not appear as a customs duty; consequently the impression is given by the minister's statement that the taxation of this country is $2,000,000 less than it really
is.	That is hardly fair. I am not going to attribute anything to the hon. Minister of Customs. He is simply giving a calculation of the customs duties; but the increased excise duty on tobacco should in fairness be included in a comparison of taxation. Then, last year we paid bounties to the extent of $2,286,289. These bounties were given in lieu of duties. The duties on iron and steel, on coal oil and on binder twine were lowered or wiped out, some of them, and then the manufacturers of these articles were given bounties. Can you tell me where the difference is? I fail to see
it.	The one is just as much a matter of taxation as the other. I was challenged a year or two ago by the Finance Minister who said that these bounties were paid out of the money that was collected through customs; but the hon. gentleman was mistaken, because these bounties are not paid out of customs duties. They are charged up to the mortgage, they are added to the delit of the country; but they are taxation against the people of this country all the same. When we find that the total amount of bounties paid since 1896 amounts to $16,326,185, I think they view the condition with alarm.
Another item which I wish to draw attention to in order to bring these tables to a fair basis is the fact that the Minister of Customs takes all the corn coming into this country from the United States, and includes it in the imports for consumption, forgetting that a large amount of that corn simply passes through this country in transit, and ought never to be taken into consideration in calculating the average rate of duties on goods, dutiable and free.

Some years ago the Finance Minister made an important statement in this House. I can excuse the hon. member for Red Deer for not having referred to it, because he was not here and possibly has never had an opportunity of seeing it. He told us practically that his new tariff was simply a readjustment, and he spoke of it thus:
It was of the -utmost importance that we should maintain a strong financial position, and in view of the uncertainties as to the amount of revenue that might be produced by this lower rate of taxation, it became necessary that we should take some steps to make good any possible loss that might result. It was thought that it might fairly be met by providing for the raising of some additional taxation in order to balance or make good the loss occasioned by the reduction of duties. It was necessary to have an increased revenue in certain directions when we were to lose revenue in other directions.
That was the policy on which the Liberal party framed its tariff. Take a little off here, and put a little on there, but always be careful that the revenue is cared for. The people had no interest, they thought, in this matter, the industries of the country were not to be considered, the sole question was to arrange so that we would get as much revenue as we did before or more. But the Minister of Customs will claim that they made a sweeping reduction in corn. I grant you they did, but when they took the duty off corn, and proclaimed throughout that they had given our farmers free corn, they simply transferred it to sugar. They largely increased the duty on sugar. Then, when a farmer went to a railway depot to get his wagon load of corn, he bought it without paying any duty; but when he went to his grocer to buy sugar he found he had two duties to pay-one the duty on corn and the other the duty on the sugar. If hon. members will analyse that statement, they will find

a great deal of truth in it. The duty may not have been exactly double, but no doubt the government were following out their system, and when they took the duty off corn they added it on to the duty on sugar. Our farmers were clamouring for free com, so they said. 'We must give them free corn, but we can fix that in such a way that they will never know, we will add it to the duty on sugar and they will never think of it. We can then tell them, when the elections are on that we gave them free corn and we need not proclaim that we doubled the duty on sugar. Our tariff is a tariff for revenue and we must have the revenue, so that if we lose our revenue on corn, we shall make it up on sugar.' And that satisfied my hon. friend from Red l)eer (Mr. Clark). In the same way they reduced the duty on wines for the benefit of some gentlemen who liked French wines for dinner, they lowered these duties away down, but on tobacco, the poor man's luxury, they put a tax over $2,000,000 in order to make up the loss bv the decrease in the duties on wine. They could not reduce the duties on wine without increasing them on something else. They took the tax off the rich man's luxury and charged it on the solace of the poor man. When my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) goes west let him tell his friend out there that he is paying the duty on the rich man's wine as well as on his own tobacco, let him give his friends an accurate understanding of what is done; but if he does, I think he will find that his friends will not vote the next time as they did on the iast occasion. [DOT]
I notice that the readjustment in the tariff in 1897 was for revenue only. The Liberals always say that their policy is a tariff for revenue. But the tariff of 1897, in very many items, remains unchanged. Our hon. friend who just sat down, (Mr. Nesbitt) said that the farmers were not worrying over the tariff. Let me tell him the reason why. It is because the agricultural schedules were not interfered with. They remained practically where they were, leaving out the two items of corn and mutton. The duty on mutton was increased from 35 per cent to 3 cents a pound, but in many other respects the tariff was not interfered with. The policy of the old Conservative party was to let in free any article which we could not produce in this country. That is the national policy. What we cannot produce, do not tax. My hon. friend shakes his head. In his opinion we should tax everything in order to get revenue. He would tax anything he could lay his hands on so long as he could get revenue. But that is not our policy. I say that what we cannot produce we ought to admit free. Under the old regime we admitted tea and coffee free, and the Liberal party dare not change that. No doubt if they thought the country would submit to it they would
tax these articles and get all the money they could out of them, but tea and coffee are two things they dare not put their hands on. Raw products, such as hides, largely brought from South America and other parts of the world, the raw material for the manufacturer, were admitted free-under the old Conservative policy, also raw ' cotton and fine wools. I am not going to say that the admission of fine wools free is the best policy at present. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) I think, will agree with me when I say that this country can to-day produce fibre wool, similar to Cape wool and Australia wool, which it could not produce 25 years ago. At present we can produce an excellent class of wool in our western country, and if encouragement were given the woollen industry, no doubt our flocks of sheep would- be enormously increased and the production of wool become one of the greatest industries of that great west. Many articles, no doubt, under the revision of the tariff were charged a lower rate, under the British preference, but that produced more revenue.
Some people have the impression that if you want more revenue, you must increase the duties. That is a great mistake. To get more revenue you must reduce the-duties. If you put a duty of 2 cents per pound on bacon and hams, a certain amount will come into this country on-which you will get a revenue. But if you raise the duty to four cents, the probability is you would exclude bacon and hams altogether and consequently get no revenue from them. The preferential tariff was framed along that line-encourage importation and get all the revenue you can even if the Canadian has to pay more for liia goods. I contend that these increased revenues, under the operation of the British preference, are at the cost of the Canadian tax-payer. When that preferential tariff was introduced, it was heralded with delight all over the country. It was heralded as a great boon to Canada. Of course, the people would naturally think that when the duties were lowered by the preference, they would get cheaper goods. But is that the sentiment of the country to-day? I would not like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, because I would not like to make him feel uncomfortable, but if the British preference was t< give us cheaper goods, what means this cry from Halifax to Vancouver that the cost of living has increased. Surely the people expected the cost of living to be reduced by that preference. Suddenly, however, it dawned on them, as matters worked out, that goods went up in price instead of coming down. The cost of living was increasing instead of getting cheaper, and that is the position in which we find ourselves to-day. Let me dwell on that for a moment. I am going to refer to the-

budget speech of the Minister of Finance to demonstrate this matter. He was very-free in making the statement, which I think will be read with a great deal of interest, that the British preference, instead of diminishing the cost of goods, has practically increased it. He told us that ' the planters in the West Indies refused to sell sugar to Canada at the same price as they sell it to the people of Great Britain. Great Britain is a free market; sugar from the West Indies goes in there without duty and so does sugar from Belgium, Russia or any other country where beet sugar is produced. But, he said, the planters in the West Indies discovered that if they were to simply follow out that rule, it would be a Canadian preference instead of a preference for them, and they, with the aid of their agents and brokers in London, made a calculation of how much it would cost the people of Canada to import sugar from foreign countries. Having done that, they enhanced their price on West India sugar for Canadians to a figure above what they charged to the people of England, knowing that the Canadians would have to pay that enhanced price, plus the preferential duty, so that instead of Canadians benefiting by this preference, in the purchase of West India sugar, they are practically losing through being compelled by the West India planters to pay a higher price. The Finance Minister, referring to the refiners of eastern Canada who were making a complaint that this thing was being done, said:
They say that there is a combination amongst the West Indian planters, among the growers of sugar in the West Indies, through their agents and brokers in London whereby the Canadian refiner is not permitted to buy that West Indian sugar upon the same terms as it is purchased by the British refiner. This question of who shall profit by the preference has been much debated. At one time the West India merchants complained that the refiners in Canada managed to take the whole preference to themselves. Now the accusation is the other way. Our Canadian refiners say that this combination so manages that it will only sell West India sugar at a price which makes the thing of really no more advantage to them than if they were to buy the foreign sugar and pay the higher duty. Of course, no matter what they pay for West Indian .sugar, they would only pay a lower rate of duty. But it is claimed that though they do not pay any more duty they are obliged to pay a higher rioe. They say that the growers in the West ndies, through a broker and agent in London, ascertain just at what price sugar can find admission into the Canadian market, and they only sell at that price, with the net result that while the British refiner who competes with the Canadian refiner in the finished product, practically buys in a free market, the Canadian refiner is only allowed to buy on terms which oblige him to pay in addition to the price of the sugar, the amount of the preferential duty.

The price of sugar referred to in the concluding words of that paragraph of the minister's speech is the enhanced price, the price of the Belgian, German, or Russian beet sugar with the full duty added. The West India planters said: 'You cannot get sugar from us unless you give an enhanced price that leaves just a little margin below the price of foreign sugar plus the full duty, which will be sufficient to induce you to purchase from us.' I ask if that is fair treatment? Is that a Canadian preference? It is a preference for the benefit of the people of the West Indies. I was ignorant enough to think, with many others, that when we1 gave a British preference we would get something out of it, and that when we gave a preference to the West Indian planters, we would derive some little benefit from it, too, but it appears that the West India planters, receive all the benefit and there is nothing in it at all for us.
Let us see how that principle will work out in the ease of linens under the British preference. The Minister of Customs practically says:	'You can buy linen in the
old country and bring it here under the preferential tariff.' Certainly you can, but when you go to the old country you mingle with as shrewd people as are to be found in the world; the linen manufacturers of Great Britain are able to form their combinations just as the Westlndia planters do. They can get together and sav:	'We will
not let the Canadians have the benefit of this preference, it must come to us.' They figure out that we cannot import linens from the United States unless we pay a duty of 30 per cent, and so they shade up the price of linen to nearly what it would cost us to import it from the United States, with 30 per cent added. Thus the British linen manufacturer will not sell to the Canadians as cheaply as they will sell to the people of the United States.
I need not carry this argument further; the same principle can be applied to cottons and to many articles eoming into Canada. The Minister of Finance demonstrated that fact to us only a few years ago. I shall use an illustration of his own, I shall reverse his illustration because it is a very curious rule that will not work both ways. Here is what the Minister of Finance said on March 23, 1900:

I shall take him at his word. He says that the price of the home product is influenced by the duty on the foreign article. That is to say. if there were 35 per cent on foreign cottons, the Canadian manufacturer would shade up his price in order to bring it very close to the figure at which the consumer in Canada could import foreign cottons and pay the duty. I grant that the principal, in fact the only precaution against that was to so increase the manufacture of cotton goods in this country that home competition would prevent a combination and keep down the price. That was the principle of the National Policy, encourage the industry and make it so strong that home competition would maintain a proner level of prices.
On coloured cotton goods coming from foreign countries the duty was much higher than when coming from Great Britain, and the Canadian manufacturer said to himself: 'Canadian consumers cannot get coloured cottons from the United States unless they pay the 35 per cent, consequently we will level up our prices to that margin.' Do you think for a moment that the British manufacturer was asleep? Do you think he was not watching our tariff? I found, when I talked with men in the old country, that they knew about as much of our tariff as we know ourselves. The manufacturer of linen in the old country can say: 'You cannot get linen from the United States or any other country unless you pay 30 per cent. True, you can get it if you buy in Britain, at a lower rate of duty, but before you can get it from us we are going to level up our
prices, we will make you pay more for the goods, and you will find, when you get your linen home, that you might just as well have bought from the United States and paid 30 per cent. 'Do you think that is not possible? I believe it is not only possible but probable. I do not take the British manufacturer to be insane. I do not believe they are doing business for the fun of it, they are doing _ business to make money, and they are going to make money, no matter who pays the piper. They are going to make money out of Canadians just as well as out of the people of other countries, and if we are simple enough to give away our market to them, give them a preference in our market, they are certainly going to take advantage of it, and I have no doubt in the world that they will do so.
What means all this cry over the country that the cost of living has increased? Go where you will, even on articles that do not come from abroad, you will find the cost of living has increased. Why? Out of sympathy. A railway tie will increase in cost as well as a yard of cotton ; it rises in sympathy with the increase in the cost of labour. There is no question in my mind that this is a solution of the whole question why goods have increased in price in Canada. Look at what we had to do for the Civil Service of Canada during the past year. Hundreds and hundreds of thousands of dollars had to be paid out to increase their salaries. Why? Because thi3 government had adopted a policy that compelled them to pay more for the requisites of their households, and it was only fair that we should come to their rescue. We had so arranged our tariff as to increase the cost of goods and it was only fair that we should come to their rescue, give them an increased salary in order to enable them to pay their way, to pay for the increased cost of living. I say this is a subject worthy of the consideration of the government. I was foolish enough, in 1897, when this policy was heralded by the government as a boon to Canada, to think it was going to be a boon to Canada. I thought that whilst we called it a British preference, it was going to be a Canadian preference. I have changed my mind. It is not a Canadian preference, it is a British preference pure and simple, and we really have no part or lot in the whole matter. Just as the West India planter says: 'Canadians are not going to get the benefit of this, they appear to have got the benefit for a year or two, but we are going to see to it now that they will not get it any longer.' So the Minister of Finance was compelled the other day to announce a policy by which he would get back for the people of Canada a small modicum of that which they ought to have had under this preference.

House in committee on Bill (No. 134) to incorporate the Canadian Medical Association.
On section 1,
This is a Dominion Medical Association that has been in existence some years, and is seeking incorporation.

It seems to me we are asked to give this association pretty large powers-to make such by-laws and rules, not contrary to law, or to the provisions of this Act, as it may deem necessary for the management of its business affairs, and especially with regard to the qualification, classification, admission and expulsion of members. Now why should an association have any right to set up a standard of qualifications for other men to get in? Suppose they set up a special examination which medical men must undergo before they can join the association, although they may hold degrees. It seems to me this is intended to make a close corporation of a section of the medical profession, and would put in their hands a power which they might use to the detriment of their brother practitioners. Suppose such an association was established in this city, and one-third of the medical men joined it, and they would make onerous laws, and prescribe qualifications which other medical men would be obliged to conform to, otherwise they could not join the society. It might not be inconsistent with the medical law of the country at the present time, but it would give them a power over otheT members of the profession in their locality which I think no association should be allowed to exercise. There must be something behind this which is not very plain. I do not see the object of it, nor do I see the wisdom of putting into the hands of any medical association such a power.

I think my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule") has misconceived the object of this clause. This is an association of medical men of the Dominion of Canada that has been in existence foT the last 40 or 50 years. They already have power to make by-laws to prescribe qualifications of membership. It is voluntary whether a man Joins or not.
It does not say what qualification, whether professional or otherwise.

You do not have to join the association unless you like, and you

become a party to the qualifications in joining the association. It is not something you are forced to join, it is quite voluntary on the part of medical men to join or not as they choose. I think they can be trusted; certainly I would not fear that they might abuse any powers entrusted to them. They already have the authority which this clause gives them.
Under what Act?

Under no Act whatever. It is voluntary on the part of medical men. They are seeking incorporation in ordeT to enable them for instance to hold property. They have not that power at the present time. They simply desire to come together for mutual advantage, to hold property, and to be able to issue a medical journal under the authority of the entire profession of the Dominion, to cement together the members ' of the profession of the several provinces. They will have interpTovincial registration, which they have not at the present time. I do not think there are any powers here at all that would be detrimental to the outside medical men. No man is compelled to come in, and if he does, he comes in with his eyes open. There are no powers sought here that the association do not exercise at the present time.
If this is the old medical association, that was provincial in its character.
No, this is the Canadian Medical Association for the Dominion, they do not interfere with any provincial association.
I am not aware of any such body holding regular meetings lately.

It meets this year in the city of Winnipeg, Dr. R. J. Blanchard is president. I am not sure whether it met last year in Winnipeg or Vancouver. It meets in a different province and a different city once a year.

If this were a medical association to cover the whole Dominion it would be more desirable and less dangerous. But, if it is only some small association, meeting in Ottawa or Toronto, such as was proposed to be incorporated a few years ago and the aim of which was, in my judgment, not of a very high nature, it would be an entirely different thing. I can see a great deal of good in the organization of the Dominion Medical Association to meet and bring together the medical men of the whole Dominion. As to the right to publish a journal, I think it is most desirable because this association would keep in view the bringing together of the medical men of the whole Dominion and would try to assimilate the laws as to the interchange of registration and such things as that.

These are all very good objects, but I have not heard of this measure before. We had a Bill of this kind to deal with once before and the fact that this has been-I was going to say-smuggled in from the Senate, makes us all the more suspicious. Very often these Bills, to which they do not want to attract too much attention, get the imprimatur of the Senate by first being put through that House and necessarily we have to look into them more carefully than we otherwise would. On section 4, existing constitution, bylaws and rules continued till changed.

We should have a copy of these by-laws for examination. Surely they might have provided them for the medical men of the House. It is treating them with rather scant courtesy to ask them to pass a thing without having seen it.

I can see no objection to permitting the unincorporated society that we are incorporating, continuing their present by-laws, until, of their own volition and by a majority of the votes, they choose to change them. Apparently the opposition comes from gentlemen who have not studied very well the history of the Dominion Medical Association. No.

I do not think it would relieve the body.

On section 7, real and personal property.

I think this last clause should be amended. It says
Provided however that the annual value of the real estate held by the association shall not exceed the sum of $50,000.
That means the annual rental of the building. A building that would rent for $50,000 would be a very large one. The Medical Association of Ontario had the worst cloud that it could have had over it from the indiscretion of the medical council in committing the association to a large expenditure for the erection of a great hall in Toronto. That was an incubus on it from which it has not yet recovered. It has broken up that unity which ought to exist between the members of the association. If you give power to put up a building of the dimensions and cost provided for in this section, the annual rental value of which would be $50,000 a year, it seems to me that you would be giving entirely too great latitude. For many of these insurance companies we put the annual value at from $10,000 to $15,000 and we think that quite enough. Five per cent on $150,000 would be $7,500. They are likely to be an itinerant body; they meet this year in Winnipeg and next year somewhere else, and if you give them the power to put up a building the annual rental of which would be $50,000 they would have to utilize it in some way to get a return for their money. I think it would be injurious to the profession to pass this clause of the Bill.

The hon. gentleman has in mind what took place in Ontario when the medical council expended a large sum of money for a building. The difference is however, that all the medical men of Ontario are compelled to pay their fees in order to keep in good standing in the council and in the opinion of a good many of the profession their representatives unwisely spent too much money in one building. I do not think it is desired by the Canadian Medical Council to put up an expensive building. You will see in the second clause that they get power to publish a medical journal and they will want a printing plant to get out bulletins, for instance, to educate the people in bygiene, and the idea is that all the property tbey may acquire for any purpose shall not exceed the sum mentioned in the clause.

That is not what the Bill says. I think it would be unwise for the association to erect a very expensive building. When we incorporate religious or educational or fraternal institutions we generally allow $10,000 as the annual value for a building, and that is considered ample.
Is not the membership in the Medical Association entirely voluntary.
Yes, but this enables them to hold too much real estate.
What difference does that make? The general Act respecting companies in Ontario fixes no limitation, and if they choose to put up an expensive building it is their own business.

I do not know what any other law may provide, but when we are passing similar Bills in this parliament we generally limit the sum to $10,000 or $15,000. The fact that the Medical Association of Ontario put up such a large building has ruined the association for years past.

The danger is that if such a large sum of money is invested in a building it may prevent medical men who are not very wealthy from joining the association because after they have joined they would be liable for whatever tax was fixed.
I would rather let the Bill stand until we get information than accept the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Sproule).
There is a difference of opinion and perhaps we should let the Bill stand so that in the meantime these gentlemen can get together and agree.

I would accept that suggestion.

' If I pay for a certain undertaking, for a certain property, or for the doing of certain work, which when completed is to be mine that is one thing; if I guarantee the cost of the doing by some other party of another piece of work that is to be directly to his benefit and directly and indirectly to my benefit, and I guarantee his paper for the amount, taking what I believe to be adequate security, that is quite another thing.

On estimates made by themselves or by some others for them.

The hon. member for North Toronto sought again to ms^ke it appear to the people of Canada that we had increased the nublic debt to a greater extent than we Mr. MILLER.
had any right to increase it, and in order to drive home that idea and to make out his case he made a comparison with the public debt of the United States and said: If you will go to the United States with its 80,000,000 or 90,000,000 of people you will find its public debt per capita is very much less of a burden. I do not know that a more unfair comparison could be instituted than a comparison between the federal debt of the United States and the federal debt of the Dominion of Canada.
Then he proceeds to give his reasons which I shall read. It is this very habit which the hon. gentleman has of arguing one way at one time under one set of circumstances and arguing another way at another time when the circumstances are entirely different, that robs him of the confidence which the people might otherwise have in him, which makes him a political impossibility, and robs him entirely of the influence with the country that a man of his educational advantages, his oratorical powers and long parliamentary experience would otherwise be entitled to enjoy. Proceeding with his argument to show why this is a wrong argument to advance he says:
I do not know that a more unfair comparison could be instituted than a comparison between the federal debt of the United States and the federal debt of the Dominion of Canada. That is exactly the position the hon. gentleman puts himself in during this present debate.
Now, if by a simple statement to-day, I can set, to a certain extent, at rest and dispose of this comparison of two things so dissimilar,
I shall feel that I have performed a duty, not only to the party in power, but to this House and to the country as well.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that if the hon. gentleman was performing a public duty in stating that argument to the House in 1889, I am surely performing a like duty when I repeat his language in 1909:
The constitution of the United States and the constitution of Canada are very different, so far as financial matters are concerned which lead to publio debts and to public expenditures.
Then the hon. gentleman proceeds to show the difference between the constitution of Canada and that of the United States. He points out:
The United States, in the first place, assumes no debts of its different states. The Dominion of Canada has assumed the debts of its provinces to the amount of $109,430,148.69. For penitentiaries, we have expended since confederation, $5,611,696.54. The penitentiaries in the United States are supported, not at the charge of the federal power, but at the charge of the different states. the assumed debts of the provinces, the subsidies paid to the provinces, the interest paid on the deht assumed from the provinces, the amount paid out for penitentiaries, the amount paid for the salaries of governors, at least half the amount she has paid for militia and defence, at least half the amount paid for the administration of justice, and the whole amount paid for immigration and quarantine, amounting in all to no less a sum than $309,860,987.40. Hon. gentlemen may treat this as a good joke, but from their point of view it is no joke, for, as soon as this gets before the people and into the minds of the people, a stock argument of the hon. gentlemen opposite will be for ever taken from them, which is their comparison on an unfair basis of the debt of the United States with ours, and always to the advantage of the United States and to our disadvantage.
Now I say again, Mr. Speaker, that if that was good argument away back in 1889, it is a fair argument to-day; and it is a very strange thing that the hon. member for North Toronto should have so completely changed his mind according as circumstances have happened to change.
Our friends on the opposite side of the House have questioned the expenditure of the government in building the Grand Trunk Pacific. I was reading lately in one of the financial journals of Canada that there would probably be opposition in this House to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but there would not be any opposition outside the House. Our friends object to the Quebec bridge, not to the cost of the bridge nor as to its necessity, but because the bridge fell down.
