Did the delegation that came down here from North York ask for the building of a canal from Lake Simcoe to Newmarket, or did they ask for the deepening of the Holland river from Lake Simcoe to Holland Landing?

That is a question that I frankly admit I am not able to answer. It has been stated in the House that gentlemen came down from the neighbourhood in which this canal was to be built and asked for its construction; whether there is any difference in detail I am not aware. But I reasoned with myself in this way: If intelligent and sane business men, one of them a Conservative member of the Ontario legislature, came down and asked for a work of this kind, what could have been their object? Did the hon. gentleman say a member of the local legislature came down here?

I trust I am not mistaken.
I understood Mr. Lennox came down, or had signed a petition.
I do not think he was a member of the local legislature at that time.

Possibly not at that time, but it is the same gentleman. I reasoned with myself in this way: These gentlemen might have asked for the construction of a large public building which might not be necessary, but would be an ornament to the locality in which they lived. But a canal Mr. MILLER.
would be an entirely different thing. A canal, if it was not to be a useful thing, would be an eyesore rather than anything that would beautify the country through which it passed. The gentleman whom I met was an honourable man; he was an intelligent man; he was a man_ wdth no personal interest, and I said to him: Tell me now confidentially what is your opinion as to the building of the Newmarket canal. That gentleman stated: Well, while I do not look with any particular degree of favour upon the building of any part of the Trent Valley canal, the Newmarket section of the canal will be just as useful as any other part of the system. If fault is found with the expenditure under the .present government, if we are told that our public debt has increased more quickly and to a greater extent than it ought to have increased, let me ask my hon. friends on the opposite side of the House and let me ask the people of Canada what they think wmuld have been the state of affairs if our good Conservative friends had been returned to power? Turn to the Halifax platform, and. we have the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) advocating-did he not?-the government ownership of railways. prudent in expenditure and careful and conservative in their purchases.

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the budget has been so comprehensive that at this stage little remains for me to add. There are still, however, a few subjects that may be of some little interest which I would like to hring to the attention of the House. One thing that has struck me very forcibly, and possibly it has struck other new members, is the bouquets that have made their appearance at different times in the House. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) and the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. W. McIntyre) on their return to the House from little political trips into their several provinces were presented with bouquets. I wondered at the time the meaning of those bouquets. It struck me at first that they were marks of appreciation on the part of their fellow members who were of their peculiar persuasion in politics; marks of especial esteem and regard; tributes to some good work accomplished by these gentlemen. But that could not have been the reason as these gentle-mn had broken the rule laid down by Liberals in my own province and in the province of Ontario. Instructions were given in these provinces to election speakers at the

time of provincial elections to say to the elctors :	Do not vote for a Liberal candidate because he is a Liberal, but vote for a Liberal candidate so as to strengthen the opposition against this Conseravtive government which is so strongly entrenched in power in order to secure good government. We heard that motto on every platform in Manitoba; that was their method of trying to wiggle in another member against the government. That policy is followed also in Ontario, but evidently when members of this federal House go to Nova Scotia and Alberta, they return here with laurels after having broken that rule laid down by the Liberals, having further strengthened the governments already too strong in those provinces. That was evidently looked upon by Liberals in this House as a reason for congratulating these members. I think it a most invidious thing that bouquets are handed out to some gentlemen and not to others. We saw an hon. gentleman who had wended his weary way from British Columbia come heTe weary and sad and worn from the efforts that he had put forward to obtain a seat by acclamation. No bouquet was handed to him. The seat he now occupies had been won in a manly way by a gentleman of the name of Sloan, but for reasons, which I fancy will appear a little later, Mr. Sloan retired in favour of the hon. the Minister of Inland Revenue and Mines (Mr. Temple-man). I myself feel like handing that hon. minister a bouquet and I would suggest a bouquet of roses as the most suitable. Roses in their beauty and fragrance would remind him of the city of Victoria which had turned him down in favour of an untried warrior on the Conservative side, even with all his prestige as minister. I would further suggest roses because with every rose go a few thorns, and these thorns in the bouquet I would give him would remind him of his feelings on the evening of the 26th of October last. The thorns might also remind the First Minister of his feelings when he heard the sorry tidings from British Columbia on that evening. The thorns also ought to have a little prick for the man from Nanaimo (Mr. R. Smith) when he remembers that he went out, fought and won his fight, and came here the accredited representative of the people, but was not thought good enough to take a portfolio as a representative in the cabinet for British Columbia. When I look at the hon. gentleman who represents British Columbia in the cabinet and think of him and his position in the government. I am reminded of a story of Richard Croker, the Tammany leader. When American horses were first run on the race courses in England Mr. Croker was very much interested. If you remember the Americans took with them to the old country their own jockey, Mr. CAMPBELL.
Todd Sloan. Sloan rode the first horse that won a race in England. The race was won by a neck, and Richard Croker was heard to exclaim:	Thank God for Sloan. Those
few wolds of thanks to the great Being, I feel sure, are reiterated most heartily by the hon. gentleman who now represents Comox-Atlin.
With the permission of the House I would like to refer to some extent to some previous debates. On the evening of March 23, the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made a solmen statement which I would like to read to this House. I must say I regret exceedingly that that right hon. gentleman is not here, because it is to him personally, perhaps, more than to the House that I would like to address my remarks. While discussing a matter that was in debate the First Minister said:
I am sorry to say that is another evidence that we are not to trust Conservatives when they pledge themselves to us as members of the House or a9 a delegation.
In other words, he stated from his place in the House that Conservatives were not worthy of credit. Now, Sir, I am a kind of a Conservative myself, and I felt at that time, as I feel now, that it was a harsh remark for the First Minister to make with regard to any loyal gentleman in this House, even though they differ with him politically. I could assure the right hon. gentleman, if he were here, that he can always trust me most implicitly, trust me to fight him as long as I have breath, as long as he follows his present methods of conducting the affairs of this country, as long as he prostitutes the great and heaven-born gifts that he possesses, a flowery language and a silver tongue, to whip, as he did on that occasion, his most unwilling followers into voting a grant of the people's hard earned money to a most useless work called the Aylesworth ditch, down which to float, or to wheel, as events will show, the Minister of Justice into his seat in this House. He can always trust me to oppose him in such projects as that, and I think I am safe in making the same promise on behalf of other hon. gentlemen on this side of the House as long as he carries on a policy of wanton waste of the public moneys that we have seen him pursuing in this House, despite all that the members of the opposition can say in the way of protest. I refer, for instance, to the buildings that were put up at Kingston for some servants of the officers there-$112,-000 for 16 houses for under-strappers of some kind of officers. Why, Sir, I want to tell you that we have some 9,000 farmers in my own riding, and they are living in houses costing from $150 to perhaps $500 or $600; and the minister who is in charge of that department asks the people's representatives, who are here tak-

ing care of the people's interests, to vote their hard earned money to build some palaces for flunkeys, and bung-starters, and I know not what. Those are some of the expenditures that I take objection to. Another thing I take objection to is the enormous waste of public money that we see voted from time to time in this House, for instance, for towers for public buildings. In one breath, the minister in charge of the department says, Canada is hard up, and we are retrenching; the next moment he asks us to vote $2,000 $3,000 or $4,000 for a tower to make a public building in Glencoe, or somewhere else, look a little better. No sooner do we vote that tower, but he asks us to vote a clock for the tower costing several thousands of dollars of the people's money; and no sooner have we voted the clock than he asks us to vote $300 or $400 to pay some fellow to wind the clock. I want to say that in matters of that kind the First Minister can absolutely and always count upon me to oppose him. He can trust me to vote against him as long as he follows his present policy of expediency instead of trying to fulfil some of his pledges.
The right hon. gentleman is credited with having a very short memory. I would like to remind him of some of the pledges he got from Conservatives, which were fulfilled, and the fulfilment of which resulted in his attaining to the position he now holds as leader of this government;
I refer to the pledges that Conservatives made to him in 1896. I am much mistaken if some of the erstwhile Conservatives who at that time made him those promises do not sit behind him now, and form part of his majority. I would ask the right hon. gentleman, if he were here, to look to his own honesty in the matter of his promises. Let him carry his memory back to 1894, I think it was, when he came to Winnipeg as leader of the great Liberal party of Canada. He told them that he came with a message to the people of the west, a message that had great bearing on the approaching election that we were all looking forward to. He made them a certain promise, a promise that I feel sure my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) would have appreciated had he been there. He got up on a public platform in Winnipeg and said to the people: I come to the west bearing you a message, I come to you preaching a gospel, a new gospel, a gospel of free trade as they have it in England. Where is it? It is gone with the breath he used in uttering these words. And still owing his position of Premier of Canada to the pledges he received from Conservatives, which were fulfilled, and to pledges he gave himself, which were unfortunately not fulfilled, he had his nerve with him, when he dared to get up and accuse Conservatives of want of credibility.
He did not say it. You had better read the whole article.
The hon. gentleman can read it for himself, it is here in the 'Hansard', I will give the page. The whole article absolutely bears; out what I said.
He didn't say it at all.

-I heard, on a previous occasion in this House, a gentleman who went even further than my hon. friend who now speaks; he refused to allow the House to credit the words that were marked in his own name. I heard the Minister of Finance, in his speech the other day, refer to the grand old policy we hear so much of, the land for the settler, as being the policy of the Liberal party. He spoke of the fact that the Conservatives had given land grants to railways, and that his government had ceased to do so. Has the hon. gentleman forgotten that there is a railroad built up through Manitoba and the IMorthwest Territories called the Canadian Northern? Has he forgotten that, from time to time since this government has been in power, that railway company has come here for an extension of time for its charters, and other extensions of rights which those charters gave it? Has he forgotten that some million acres of land have been given to the Canadian Northern by this government, because that is an absolute fact, and he cannot deny it, nor can any one deny it with truth. Has he forgotten, Sir, with regard to his policy of the land for the settler, a fact which is fairly well known and has been fairly well advertised that his government gave 250,000 acres of land to a company principally of Americans for $1 an acre? When that deal was consummated the poor settler, the man who gives the land value, had to pay from $5 to $15 an acre for the same land and the quality of which- had not changed in any way although the land had changed from the ownership of the people to the ownership of a band of American speculators. He has perhaps forgotten all that was said at that time with respect to the politicians who took an active part in putting through the deal. It was stated and it is believed in the west that a certain politician who still has a seat in this House received from the Saskatchewan Valley and Manitoba Land Company a certificate of stock to the amount of $50,000 signed in blank and handed to him for his share in putting the deal through.
I do not think that a charge of that kind can be made against a member of this House.

I would have very much preferred to have made the remark in the presence of the gentleman I specially refer to.

Mr.' FIELDING. The hon. gentleman would not be at liberty to make it in the absence of the gentleman referred to. He can make an accusation against a gentleman and have it tried out, but be cannot make such a remark in the way he suggests.
I think the language which he has used is quite permissible. He says that it has been said. We often hear what is current rumour quoted in this House.

Well, rumour is quoted
very often in the House.
Perhaps it would meet the views of the hon. Minister of Finance if I would say that it is common report among the people.

I suppose it is possible for me to withdraw the words without withdrawing the meaning?

Yes.

At the same time that these charges were current in regard to the hon. gentleman I spoke of there were other charges made, they were made so late as last summer on the public platform in Saskatchewan and they were made by one of the late directors of the company to the effect that the man I now speak of, whose name I have no object in concealing-his name is Walter Scott-when he was a member of this House, accepted, for his efforts on behalf of putting that Bill through, a certificate of stock of the Saskatchewan Valley and Manitoba Land Company signed in blank to the extent of $10,000. That is common report. It was said on every public platform in Saskatchewan that I had the felicity to be on. It was denied, it is true by the Hon. Walter Mr. CAMPBELL.
Scott, but he took very good care never to deny that accusation when made by the man that I have mentioned. I repeat, it was common report. I think that possibly every minister in this House knew the report. But, I can say more than that. I know the man who handed the stock to Walter Scott, and I saw all the evidence in the matter. This government, through its Finance Minister, says that is good business. The Finance Minister says it is good business to give land belonging to the people to American speculators for $1 an acre, and whatever perquisites can be got from them on the side. He says it is good business to let these American speculators come into Canada, exploit the country and sell to the poor farmer, for from $5 to $15 an acre, land which they are able to get for $1 an acre. Then, this hon. gentleman goes around the country saying: the land for the people, not the speculators, is our motto. I would point out further to hon. gentlemen on that side of the House, and I would bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance, that for years and years the Manitoba government had a claim upon what is called the Manitoba and North Western Eailway lands lying between Lake Manitoba and Lake Winnipeg. They were to get every odd numbered section in every odd numbered township in every odd numbered range until they got the full complement of 250,000 acres. For years and years the Manitoba government applied to get that land so that they could do something with it, so that it would be an available asset, but they could not get one acre of it surveyed and they could not get any right to it until it was surveyed. Finally, the Canadian Northern people-I do not know whether they called themselves the Canadian Northern Eailway Company or Mackenzie & Mann, or under what name they operated-came to the Manitoba government and said: We will give you $400,000 cash for your claim to that land which you cannot get. They simply had to sell their equity to Mackenzie & Mann. Mackenzie & Mann came down to this government, and within a few months this government handed over to them, in lieu of the land which is very poor, for the most part, being covered with water, scrub and stone though there are some townships of first class land admixed	through	it, the best
land that Mackenzie & Mann could select out in Saskatchewan. Yet, my hon. friend says :	The land for the people.
Who are the people ? In that case the people were Mann & Mackenzie. The hon. gentleman says that their policy is not to give land to the railway companies, that their policy is to keep the land for the settler. Is he not aware that his own government gave 20 square miles for every

mile of road constructed by the Canadian Northern Railway Company from Erwood to the Pas Mission amounting to over a million acres? Instead of giving them wild land there of comparatively little value, they gave Mann & Mackenzie the same right in that case as they did in the other to pick out their land in Saskatchewan. Yet the hon. gentleman says: 'The land for the settler.'
Frequent reference has been made to the land grant given to the Canadian Pacific Railway by the Conservative government, and at this late hour I shall not enter into a lengthy discussion of that question. There has been a great deal said about the fact that the Conservative government did a great deal for the Canadian Pacific Railway and no one can deny that it gave that railway company a tremendous land grant. But in those days the land was worth comparatively nothing and had not the Canadian Pacific Railway built into that western country the land never would have been worth anything. A few years before the Canadian Pacific Railway went into Winnipeg you could have bought the whole town site for $5,000, but to-day it is worth millions and millions. It was the advent of the Canadian Pacific Railway into that country that made the land worth anything whatever. And, Sir, speaking of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I am reminded of the question brought up by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) in connection with the permission given that company by the government recently to increase their borrowing powers. In that regard let me say that the opinion voiced by the hon. member (Mr. Maclean) and by the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. McIntyre) and by the hon. member for Assin-iboia (Mr. Turiff) is the opinion held by 99 per cent of the people of the west. The Minister of Justice told us that the contract made between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway was vastly in favour of the railway company and against the people, but he said:	'I hold that a
contract is a sacred thing and so long as its true intent and meaning is lived up to it cannot be infringed upon. 'Well, I believe that no sane man who was in this House in 1881 when that contract was made, believed anything else than that the exemption clause was to expire in twenty years from the date of the contract and 'Hansard' shows that every member of parliament at that date believed that such was the true intent and meaning of the contract, outside perhaps of lawyers' quibbles. That being so, this government was remiss_ in its duty to the people when on the various occasions that the Canadian Pacific Railway came asking for favours it did not say to the Canadian Pacific Railway : ' This is the true intent and meaning of your contract; we want you to abrogate that ex-154
eruption even though you have perhaps a legal right to it; you are asking something from us now and we will not give it to you unless you show the people of the west that their interest is your interest, and that you will not shelter yourselves behind a legal quibble with regard to this contract.' The government did not do that, and the government was remiss in its duty. As my hon. friend from Strathcona well said: 'How would any man in the east like if he were compelled not only to pay his own taxes, but to pay the taxes of his neighbour,' and that is absolutely the condition in every settlement in the west where Canadian Pacific Railway lands are located in any quantity. The Canadian Pacific Railway refuses to pay taxes, it refuses to do any road work, its land grows in value from day to day through the toil of the poor farmers in the neighbourhood, and as guardians of the public interest the government was more than remiss in its duty to those people that it did not insist on a quid pro quo from the Canadian Pacific Railway when it came seeking favours. Now. Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to another matter, and I am going to refer to it largely because, like every Scotchman, I hate to be dared to do or not to do anything. The hon. gentleman from Regina (Mr. Martin) speaking with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific loan, said there was no member from the west who dare oppose it. Well, were he here to-night I would let him know that I dare oppose it and I will tell him why. The primary reason is that the Grand Trunk Pacific has not lived up to its contract with the government, and to prove that I will quote from the remarks of the supporters of the government when the contract was under discussion.

I call the attention of tHe hon. member to the fact that the question is still on the Order Paper for the second reading of the Bill to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. There is great latitude allowed in the budget debate, but it is not permitted to discuss a question which is still on the Order Paper.

I bow to your decision, Sir, but I had to tell your deputy on one occasion that what was flesh for one ought to be flesh for another; and so far, other members who have taken part in this debate have been allowed to refer to this subject. However, I do not wish to insist against your ruling.
I would not like the hon. member to think that I am unjust to him.
I do not think that at all, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: There have been various reference to the Grand Trunk project during the debate, but I do not think any hon. gentleman has discussed the loan.

It is clearly in order that my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) should point out in this debate that the Grand Trunk Pacific have not carried out their contract, which is a different thing altogether from discussing the loan.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I will have much pleasure in leaving the loan alone for the present, and I only wish that you would rule that the government also should leave it alone. I was going to point out that the hon. member for Brandon said :
We make a clear-cut proposition embodied in a contract signed and sealed with a reputable corporation of great resources which is going ahead with this work as rapidly as possible.
In his opinion the Grand Trunk Pacific Company was a reputable corporation of great resources. The hon. Minister of Finance, if I may quote him, referring to the Grand Trunk corporation, said:
We have not been content that they should stand behind it. We have required, and they have readily consented, that they shall be in it and of it and form the whole thing.
I want to point out that they are very much in it-that they need $5,000,000 in their own business to pay themselves. That is why they are in it. They are looked upon as a company of great resources, and because they are in it and of it and form the whole thing, therefore Canada should respond to their call when they do call. I would point out to those gentlemen who think so highly of the resources of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, this fact, that these people, who are in it and of it and the whole thing, owe Canada, and have owed Canada for years, $50,000,000, with interest, and Canada cannot get a cent; and still we are asked to bank for these people. I think perhaps the fact that they owe that $50,000,000, with interest, has something to do with their trouble in financing for themselves. My opinion of the trouble with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and their failure to carry out their contract with the people of this country, is this. It was pointed out by the First Minister, by his aides and his general help, that this was a colonization road-that when it got into the western country it was going to open up new country. What has it done in that respect? In the province of Manitoba you can stand anywhere on the Grand Trunk Pacific and throw a stone on to either of the old roads, the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern. Is that carrying out the promise made to the people by the government on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific? That to my mind is breaking the contract; ana many hundreds of farmers, all through that western country are in need of railways to open up the particular districts in which they live. I Mr. FIELDING.
heard the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) make the remark that in his riding the Grand Trunk Pacific paralleled another road for over eighty miles. Is that making a colonization road to open up a new country and benefit the farmers ?
Will the hon. gentleman kindly give us the date when the hon. member for Assiniboia made that statement?-because the Grand Trunk Pacific dees not go into his riding at all.

I was perhaps wrong in quoting the hon. memuer for Assiniboia just in the way I did. To correct myself and to put myself absolutely in the right, I may say that his argument was this, that it ought to have come through his riding, and instead of doing so it had paralleled another road within a stone's throw. My own opinion with regard to this Grand Trunk Pacific project is this, that the construction company behina it, call it what you will, has made up its mind that it is going to make its rake-off now out of Canada. Everything it sells to Canada, from town sites down to ties, is sold at from ten dewn to three prices over proper values. They are going to make all they can out of Canada, and when they have built a road which	will have	cost
so much that it will be almost impossible to operate it at a profit, they will band it back to Canada and say: ' HeTe is your road, run it yourself.' For example, I will instance the little matter of ties, millions of which are used. In the season before last ties were made and laid down on the right of way of the Transcontinental Railway by the contractors, who made money doing it, at from 21 to 28 cents each, and Canada pays for those same ties in the neighbourhood of 60 cents each. Nobody in this House can refute that. Perhaps in a few isolated cases, when some party heeler required a long price, a little more was paid: but the great bulk of the ties on the Transcontinental Railway were laid down on the right of way at the prices I have stated.

On the section eastward from Fort William-the eastern division.
Another matter of policy of the government that I would like to take a little cognizance of is the matter of deferred elections. I have had some personal knowledge of this matter, both on one side and the other, and if any man in this House is an authority on the subject I think I am. I had a deferred election in 1892 over practically the same territory that I now represent in this House. In 1896 I had the same experience. In 1899 I did not happen to be there, and a friend of the same stripe of

politics as myself had the experience. In 1904 I had the same experience over the same territory, but for the federal house. On that occasion there was more time between the date of the issue of the writ and the date of the election than there was in the last election, when we did not have a deferred election. The reason why we did not have a deferred election this time was perhaps this, that the best thinking Liberals in Dauphin constituency had got tired of deferred elections; they had got tired of being disfranchised, and they told the gentleman who was representing the Liberal interest that if he held a deferred election he could not count on their support.
That was perhaps one reason. Another was that I had the pleasure of travelling with the returning officer a few days before, when he had to make known whether there was to be a deferred election or not. The conversation turned on that possibility, and I advised him, as a friend, having heard the rumour, that if he did not want to take a prominent part in a hanging bee, he had better not have a deferred election.
I mention this to show the feeling of the people in that country on that point. Neither Conservatives or Liberals out there want deferred elections. We want the use of our franchise and are prepared to use it in the proper way. In 1899, another gentleman had the pleasure of contesting a deferred election. On that occasion it was a provincial election and this man, who was a prominent worker for the Liberals in Winnipeg, went out on a specia train. I hope my non. friend from Rainy River, (Mr. Conmee) will not get angry with me for speaking of special trains. On that train he had 50 or 60 men to whom he paid $2 a day and provided them with all the whisky they wanted besides what they required to eat. He took them up-I had the story from himself-into	a district
where there were no actual settlers, and voted them time and again until he piled up 400 of a majority for the government candidate. His employers were gentlemen known to both sides, and if any one is ainxious for the names I shall be pleased to whisper them to him. I can assure you that if the Liberal candidate at that time were here, he would not want to hear the names. That is the great danger in deferred elections. The government have the leverage by running all the party heelers into the particular districts, even if there be an election held and it does not go by acclamation, and in this way they can smother the voice of the people. I would be in favour of this House setting the example of legislation in such a way as to prevent the holding of deferred elections, which they could easily do. In Manitoba there are certain districts in which it has become the fashion to hold I54i
deferred elections. That happened in my own case in the last provincial election. Although I tried personally in every way possible to obviate the necessity, still for certain reasons, owing to the state of the law on elections, it was not possible to get time enough to hold the contest on the same day as the others. Perhaps while that was not an unmixed benefit to my opponent, because I believe it saved him expenses and his deposit of $200 as the seat was given to me by acclamation, this government should set an example in that particular matter to the provinces, and I feel sure that if it did, the provinces would have no reason in the world for not following suit.
Another matter to which I wish to bring your attention is something which occurs on account of deferred elections. That is explained in a letter, of which I shall give a paraphrase to the House. I do not wish to read the letter itself, because I do not intend to lay it on the table, but I shall give the exact meaning. The letter was to the following effect:
I write to ask if you will not come down and use your influence to call Glen off. He is very stubborn, and no one here can do anything with him.
* This was written in 1904, before the election, and it was written to a gentleman who had been actively concerned in political interests with the writer or his close friend. The writer went on to say:
In any case, I think we can heat him, hut you know you never can tell what these damned Grits will do.
This was written by a Liberal candidate, and it will not surprise you to learn that I have no wish to endorse his language, having been brought up in the Presbyterian church myself. But I often wonder who were the gentlemen who were stigmatised by that unhappy epithet. Did he have in his mind, I wonder, the right hon. the Prime Minister or any of his cabinet, or the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton)? Or did he just mean the honest and decent Liberal electors? I think perhaps that is really what he meant. Being a turncoat Tory himself, having been a Tory for years, so long as the flesh-pots were in charge of the Conservative party, and having changed his politics in 1896 because the flesh-pots still had attractions for him, possibly I am right when I say it was the honest Liberal electorate he was referring to. But if there were no deferred elections, a letter such as that would be impossible.
I just want to say a word with regard to my hon. friend who is asleep here, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). Knowing him as I do, I know that anything ,1 say will not be offensive to him. When

he spoke yesterday I listened to him attentively, and do yon know the thought that flashed across my mind was this :	' Here
is another maverick.' Perhaps you do not know what a maverick is. It is an unbranded steer running on the range, owned by nobody and subject to be caught at any time and branded, and the ownership would then be in the proprietor of the brand. My hon. friend was wandering around talking free trade and imagining he was talking for those gentlemen over there. His speech was all right if he had only brought it to a logical conclusion. He talked free trade, and then he talked of what the government had done for free trade, and admitted that the Conservatives had done more to reduce the tariff really than had those so-called free traders. And he went on to speak of inconsistency in politics When he considers those two facts, and the conclusion he came to in regard to the lowering of the tariff being greater on this side than on that, there is only one thing for him to do, and that is to rub off the hair-brand he got since he came down here and fall in line with the people he knows are honest. He knows that on that side they are not honest because on one particular occasion they were so dishonest that he went out and would not vote for them. He felt, as I say, lost. He is a free trader; there is no free trade in Canada.
Can the hon. member recall a single phrase in which I mentioned free trade?

I am not referring to what he specifically mentioned in the way of free trade because I realize that since he came down to this House there are some things which he must not mention in a Liberal camp. But the hon. gentleman cannot deny that he is one of the most ardent free traders in Canada. On this side of the House, Sir, we call a spade a spade, we believe in protection and call it protection. The other people believe in protection but they call it by any name under the sun that they think will hood-wink the people. I believe in protection and I believe in this party because they enunciate clearly and honestly what their policy is in that regard and they are willing always to stand and fall by it.
I listened to the splendid logical argument laid before this House on the matter of imperial defence or aid to imperial defence delivered by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Poster). It was found fault with by the hon. gentleman who leads the House. Why? Because it was not concrete. That is the fault he found with it and what did he give us? He gave us verbiage, which means nothing. Why, Sir, Mr. CAMPBELL.
it is time for this House to realize that the whole world is looking to Canada in this particular matter. I say the whole world and I mean it. Why these little Japanese with their civilization 4,000 years older than ours in some matters of esthetics and the arts, have come to realize in the last few years that painting and ornamental work of that kind does not bring them anything, they have become ambitious to take a position in the world and have taken a position by defeating great Russia. The fact that they defeated Russia has stimulated them to further aspirations, there is no doubt about that, they are looking around for fresh worlds to conquer, they are watching to see what Canada is going to do, when the motherland is calling. Then there is Russia, she is watching as we all know, to see if anything will befall the navy of Great Britain. If anything occurs to the navy of Great Britain, I am of the opinion that the next day Russia will be marching across the borders into northern India. Germany is watching to see what Canada will do. Why? Because she has an idea that if she can only beat England on the sea she has the supremacy of the world. She is watching to see if Great Britain has her colonies at her back, she is watching to see whether the Germans, who have come out here by thousands, are ready to support loyally the country of their choice and their adoption. France is watching for the same reason that all the minor powers in Europe are watching, watching on account of her commerce for one reason, because she knows that the naval power of Great Britain has stood for the safe commerce of the world, has stood for the safe commerce of all the smaller countries, knows that the navy of Great Britain has not been maintained and brought to its present standard because Great Britain desired to go out to conquer new worlds, but simply because Great Britain believed that as long as she held the supremacy of the seas, the commerce of all kinds from the smallest nation to the greatest nation was safe. France is looking to this colony to see what it will do. France does not forget that on this side of the Atlantic are the descendants of Frenchmen in their thousands, she looks to them to see whether the old French chivalry, the loyalty to the flag which protects them, is dead in the descendants of the men who came over from beauteous France. She is looking to see if chivalry died in this country when fell Montcalm.
I think further that we ought to remember that in Great Britain there are hundreds of thousands, nay millions of people who for all those decades have been paying ' with a smile ' for the protection of Can-

ada as well as other colonies, they have been paying their taxes, and it has been hard to pay them, with a smile, because they knew it was Great Britain's colony, it was the daughter of the great mother, whom they were helping to protect. Those people are looking to us to see whether we are going to respond to the call, if we are not going to show that we were ready to help our brothers across the sea in bearing the burden they have to beaT on our account. All through Canada the people have been looking to see if anything definite is going to be done. Every board of trade from the Atlantic to the Pacific has been passing resolutions to that end, to have Canada show herself, show her hand, show her willingness to come out in the open and say:	We are with the mother
country. Send the message to Great Britain. ' You can call on us for what you want and we are behind you.'
1 was more than surprised to hear the hon. gentleman from Nanaimo (Mr. R. Smith) speak in such a cold-b'ooded way about gathering up gear and gvlting rich. No matter how rich we got, if anything should happen to the navy of Great Britain, where are we at with all our richness? The hon. gentleman who represents in this House the hardy men of the Yukon came here and made a cold-blooded speech on this subject. Knowing the people of the north country as I do, 1 declare that his sentiments as expressed in this House are not the sentiments of the men who have gone into that north country and taken their lives in their hands from day to day. I hope the First Minister will reconsider his reply of two or three days ago with regard to aid in the matter of Dreadnoughts. I hope he will consider that even although he cannot trust me to back him up in many of the things he does, there is one thing in which I and every Conservative would support him, loyally and enthusiastically, that is, if he would come to this House and give us a part in saying what we will do for the mother country and for the empire. Had he been here I would have taken pleasure in telling him that it is my opinion that this is the hour and he is the man, and all Canada is looking to him.
